title: Circuit switching, packet switching
overview: Topic 14.2 compares the two ways of carrying data across a network made of many linked switching nodes. Circuit switching sets up a dedicated path between sender and receiver before any data is sent, keeps it for the whole communication and then releases it, which is how the traditional telephone network works. Packet switching sets up no path: the message is split into packets, each with a header holding the addresses and a sequence number, and every packet is routed independently, so packets can take different routes, arrive out of order and be reassembled at the destination. You need the benefits and drawbacks of each method and where each is suitable, the function of a router in packet switching (reading the destination address, consulting its routing table, choosing the next hop, decreasing the hop limit), and a step-by-step account of how a message crosses a network such as the internet, including what happens when a packet is lost.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of circuit switching: its benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable.
Show understanding of packet switching: its benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable.
Show understanding of the function of a router in packet switching.
Explain how packet switching is used to pass messages across a network, including the internet.

definitions.definition: A method in which a dedicated communication path (circuit) is established between sender and receiver before transmission, is used only by them for the whole communication, and is released at the end.
A method in which a message is broken into packets that are sent independently across a shared network, possibly by different routes, and reassembled in order at the destination.

A small unit of data sent across a packet-switched network, made of a header (control information such as addresses and sequence number), a payload (part of the message) and often a trailer (error-checking value).
A device that connects networks and forwards each packet towards its destination by reading the destination IP address and choosing the next hop from its routing table.
A table held by a router that maps destination networks to the next hop (and the interface to use), often with a cost for each route, updated as links fail or become congested.
One step of a packet's journey, from one router or host to the next.
A value in the packet header that each router decreases by one; when it reaches zero the packet is discarded, so packets that cannot be delivered do not circulate for ever.
A number in the header giving a packet's position in the original message, so the receiver can put packets back in order and notice any that are missing.
A packet-switched service in which the receiver acknowledges packets, so the sender knows what has arrived and resends anything unacknowledged (as TCP does).
A packet-switched service in which packets are sent without checking that the receiver is ready and without any acknowledgement of delivery (as IP does).

sections.title: Two ways to carry data across a network
content: A large network is a mesh of links joined by switching nodes (telephone exchanges or routers). Circuit switching reserves a complete path through the nodes before sending, and all data follows it. Packet switching reserves nothing: the data is split into packets and each node decides, packet by packet, where to send each one next.
bullets: Circuit switching: dedicated path set up in advance, used for the whole communication, released at the end.
Packet switching: no set-up; message split into packets, each routed independently over shared links.
Circuit switching is implemented at the physical layer; packet switching at the network (Internet) layer.
The internet is packet switched; the traditional telephone network is circuit switched.

sections.title: Circuit switching: how it works
content: When a call is made, the exchanges connect a chain of links from caller to receiver. The circuit is established before transmission starts and released once it ends. While it exists, the whole bandwidth of the circuit is reserved for this one communication, whether data is flowing or not, and all data is transferred over the same route at a fixed data rate, so it arrives in order and needs no reassembly.
bullets: 1 The sender identifies the intended receiver.
2 The network checks that the receiver is available and ready to accept data.
3 A dedicated circuit/channel is established across the network before transmission starts.
4 Data is transferred using the whole bandwidth, all over the same route.
5 The circuit is released once transmission ends.

sections.title: Circuit switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
content: The benefits come from having the path to yourself: the whole bandwidth, a fixed data rate, data in order and no reassembly. The drawbacks come from the same reservation: set-up takes time and money, nobody else can use the circuit even when it is idle, a single route means no alternative if a link fails, and a single route is easier to intercept. It suits long, continuous, real-time communication.
bullets: Benefit: data arrives in order, so no time is needed to reassemble packets.
Benefit: the whole bandwidth is available to the one communication.
Benefit: simple method; fixed data rate along the same path, so no data is lost or disordered.
Drawback: nobody else can use the circuit even when it is idle; bandwidth cannot be shared.
Drawback: less secure, because only one route is used, which is easier to intercept.
Drawback: no alternative route if a link fails.
Drawback: significant cost and time to establish the dedicated connection.

Applicable when a dedicated path must be kept for a whole call, the whole bandwidth is needed or communication is real time: voice calls, live video, private data networks, long continuous communication.

examples.label: How much reserved capacity does a phone call waste?
examples.content:
A digital voice circuit reserves 64 kbit/s for a 10-minute call.
One person is speaking for only 40% of the time in each direction.

Capacity reserved in one direction = 64,000 bit/s x 600 s = 38,400,000 bits
Unused (60% of the time)            = 38,400,000 x 0.6    = 23,040,000 bits
                                    = 2,880,000 bytes, about 2.88 MB

In a circuit-switched network nobody else can use that idle capacity.
In a packet-switched network other users' packets would fill the gaps.

(Figures checked by script.)

sections.title: Packet switching: breaking a message into packets
content: The sender splits a large message into smaller chunks of equal size (the last may be shorter) called packets. Each packet has a header and a payload, and the header carries enough information for the packet to be delivered on its own: the TCP header adds ports and the sequence number, the IP header adds the source and destination IP addresses and hop limit. Smaller packets mean more header overhead but cheaper resending.
bullets: Packet = header + payload (the part of the message it carries).
Source IP address: where the packet came from, so replies and resend requests can be returned.
Destination IP address: where the packet is going (read by every router).
Sequence number: the packet's position in the message, for reassembly.
Total number of packets / packet length: so the receiver knows when the message is complete.
Hop limit (TTL): how many more routers the packet may pass through.
Checksum: lets the receiver detect a corrupted packet.

examples.label: How many packets, and how much header overhead, for a 50,000-byte file?
examples.content:
Each packet has a 40-byte header (20-byte IP + 20-byte TCP headers).

Payload 1,000 bytes per packet:
  packets  = 50,000 / 1,000 = 50
  headers  = 50 x 40 = 2,000 bytes; total sent = 52,000 bytes
  overhead = 2,000 / 52,000 = 3.85% of the bytes sent
  one lost packet costs 1,040 bytes to resend

Payload 500 bytes per packet:
  packets  = 50,000 / 500 = 100
  headers  = 100 x 40 = 4,000 bytes; total sent = 54,000 bytes
  overhead = 4,000 / 54,000 = 7.41% of the bytes sent
  one lost packet costs only 540 bytes to resend

Smaller packets: more overhead, but cheaper retransmission.
(All figures checked by script.)

sections.title: How packet switching passes a message across the internet
content: Each packet goes to the local router, which reads the destination IP address and forwards it; every router repeats this, so the route is built hop by hop. Routing depends on the network traffic, so packets of one message can take different routes and arrive out of order, sharing links with other users' packets. The receiver buffers them, reorders them by sequence number and checks them; if a packet is missing or corrupted a resend request is sent and only that packet is resent.
bullets: 1 A large message is split into smaller packets of equal size.
2 Each packet gets a header (source and destination IP addresses, sequence number) and a payload.
3 Each packet is dispatched independently and given its own route, depending on network traffic.
4 Routers read the destination address and forward each packet to the next hop.
5 Packets arrive out of order and are reassembled into the original message using sequence numbers.
6 If packets are missing or corrupted, a resend request is sent for those packets only.

examples.label: Trace: reassembling 'MEET AT 11:30 GATE' from six 3-character packets
examples.content:
Sent: 1 'MEE'  2 'T A'  3 'T 1'  4 '1:3'  5 '0 G'  6 'ATE'

Arrival order | Buffer holds (by sequence number) | Complete?
3 'T 1'       | 3                                 | no
1 'MEE'       | 1, 3                              | no
4 '1:3'       | 1, 3, 4                           | no
2 'T A'       | 1, 2, 3, 4                        | no
6 'ATE'       | 1, 2, 3, 4, 6                     | no, 5 missing
(no acknowledgement for 5 reaches the sender, which times out and resends it)
5 '0 G'       | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6                  | yes

Reassembled in sequence order: 'MEET AT 11:30 GATE' (18 characters)
(Checked by running the reassembly code below.)

sections.title: Connectionless and connection-oriented service: dealing with lost packets
content: Packets are lost when router queues overflow, when noise corrupts them (checksum fails) or when the TTL reaches zero. A connectionless service (IP, UDP) sends without acknowledgements. A connection-oriented service (TCP) has the receiver acknowledge packets; the sender resends any packet not acknowledged before a timeout, and duplicates are discarded by sequence number. Real-time applications often prefer connectionless delivery, because a resent packet would arrive too late.
bullets: Causes of loss: congestion (full router buffers), corruption (checksum fails), TTL reaching zero.
Connectionless (IP, UDP): no acknowledgement; lower overhead.
Connection-oriented (TCP): acknowledgements; resend after timeout; duplicates discarded by sequence number.
Only the lost packet is resent, not the whole message.

examples.label: Receiver reassembling packets and reporting missing ones
examples.content:
# Receiver side of packet switching: put packets back in order, spot any that are missing
def reassemble(arrived, total):
    buffer = {}
    for seq, data in arrived:
        buffer[seq] = data                      # store each packet under its sequence number
    missing = [n for n in range(1, total + 1) if n not in buffer]
    if missing:
        return None, missing                    # ask the sender to retransmit these
    return "".join(buffer[n] for n in range(1, total + 1)), []

arrived = [(3, "T 1"), (1, "MEE"), (4, "1:3"), (2, "T A"), (6, "ATE")]
print(reassemble(arrived, 6))
arrived.append((5, "0 G"))                      # the resent packet 5 arrives
print(reassemble(arrived, 6))

# Output:
# (None, [5])
# ('MEET AT 11:30 GATE', [])

sections.title: The function of a router in packet switching
content: A router connects networks. For each packet it examines the header and reads the destination IP address, then consults its routing table, which holds for each destination the netmask, the gateway (next hop), the available hops and the status of the routes. It decides on the next hop (the best route currently available), decreases the TTL (discarding the packet at zero) and sends the packet on in a new frame. Routers share route information, so they detect changes in the network such as a failed link and send data another way. No router knows the whole route, only the next hop.
bullets: Examines the packet's header and reads the destination IP address.
Has access to a routing table: netmask, gateway (next hop), available hops and status of the routes.
Decides on the next hop (best route) and sends the packet on its next hop.
Decreases the TTL; discards the packet if it reaches zero.
Detects changes in the network (failures, congestion) and sends data another way, so it still arrives.
Connects different networks (e.g. a LAN to the internet).

examples.label: A router choosing the next hop, and a packet running out of hops
examples.content:
Routing table of router R2 (simplified):
Destination network | Next hop | Cost
198.51.100.0/24     | R4       | 2
198.51.100.0/24     | R3       | 5
203.0.113.0/24      | R5       | 3
default             | R1       | -

Packet for 198.51.100.40 -> best entry is next hop R4 (cost 2).
If the R2-R4 link fails, the R4 entry is removed and the next packet goes via R3.

Hop limit trace: a packet leaves with TTL 5 but its route needs 7 routers.
Router | TTL after decrease | Action
R1     | 4                  | forward
R2     | 3                  | forward
R3     | 2                  | forward
R4     | 1                  | forward
R5     | 0                  | discard (the sender's TCP will time out and resend)

(TTL trace checked by script.)

sections.title: Packet switching: benefits, drawbacks and where it is applicable
content: Links are occupied only while packets cross them, so many users share the same channel at once and no dedicated path is needed. Each packet is routed independently, so packets can be rerouted around faults, and because a message's packets take different routes it is harder to intercept the whole message. Missing packets are detected by sequence number and resent, so the message arrives accurate and complete. The costs are header overhead, time to reassemble packets, delays while errors are corrected, and more complex protocols, which make it unsuitable for real-time communication.
bullets: Benefit: a dedicated path does not need to be established.
Benefit: packets can be rerouted if problems arise (overcomes faulty lines).
Benefit: more secure, because packets take different routes, so the whole message is harder to intercept.
Benefit: allows simultaneous use of the channel by multiple users; bandwidth is shared.
Benefit: accuracy and completeness: missing or corrupted packets are detected and a resend request is sent.
Drawback: significant time is taken to reassemble packets at the destination.
Drawback: time delays while errors are corrected, caused by network problems.
Drawback: requires complex protocols for delivery.
Drawback: unsuitable for real-time transmission applications.
Applicable to: digital data networks such as the internet; large files that do not need live streaming; high-volume data; when the whole bandwidth is not needed; email, text messages, documents.

sections.title: Choosing the switching method for a given application
content: Ask whether the data must arrive with a steady delay (real time) and whether traffic is continuous or bursty. Real-time, continuous traffic points to circuit switching; delay-tolerant, bursty traffic points to packet switching. Justify with dedicated or shared bandwidth, order of arrival, rerouting or security, not with a bare 'faster'.
bullets: Real-time, continuous, order-critical (phone call, live video conference): circuit switching.
Complete but not time-critical, bursty (email, web page, file download, software update): packet switching.
Guaranteed capacity between two fixed sites (leased line): circuit switching.
Many users with occasional traffic sharing one network (the internet): packet switching.

examples.label: Four scenarios with justified choices
examples.content:
1 A hospital sends patients' scan images to a specialist overnight.
  Packet switching: must arrive complete and correct but a short delay does not matter;
  lost packets are resent; bandwidth is shared with other traffic.

2 A live video interview between two TV studios.
  Circuit switching: needs constant bandwidth and a steady delay; frames must arrive
  in order without gaps, and a dedicated circuit gives exactly that.

3 A school's email system.
  Packet switching: email is bursty and not real-time; packets can arrive out of order
  and be reassembled; no need to tie up a circuit between messages.

4 Two bank branches that transfer data all day and need guaranteed capacity.
  Circuit switching (a leased line): continuous traffic, so the reserved bandwidth
  is rarely idle, and the capacity is never shared with other users.

formulas.label: Number of packets
formulas.expression: Packets = ROUND UP (message size / payload per packet)
formulas.note: The last packet may carry less than a full payload.

formulas.label: Header overhead
formulas.expression: Overhead % = (packets x header size) / (message size + packets x header size) x 100
formulas.note: The fraction of the bytes sent that are headers rather than data.

rows: Dedicated path set up before sending and kept until the end

diagram.title: A message crossing the internet by packet switching
nodes: Message split into numbered packets with source and destination IP addresses
Each packet sent independently to the local router
Each router reads the destination address, decreases TTL and picks the next hop from its routing table
Packets take different routes and arrive out of order

analysisChains.title: Why the internet uses packet switching
steps: Most internet traffic, such as web pages and email, is bursty: short transfers separated by long gaps
A reserved circuit would sit idle during those gaps, so each user would waste most of the capacity reserved for them
With packet switching the gaps are filled by other users' packets, so the same links serve far more users
And because each packet is routed independently, traffic flows round failed or congested links instead of connections being dropped
analysisChains.evaluation: Efficiency and resilience outweigh the costs of header overhead and variable delay for data that must arrive complete but not instantly; real-time traffic is the case where those costs start to matter.

analysisChains.title: Why a voice call suits circuit switching better
steps: Speech must be played back continuously with a short, steady delay
On a packet-switched network each packet can take a different route and meet different queues, so delay varies and packets arrive out of order
Waiting to reorder them or resend lost ones adds delay, and a resent packet may arrive after it was needed
A circuit gives the call dedicated bandwidth with every sample arriving in order after the same delay
analysisChains.evaluation: Circuit switching gives better call quality, but the reserved capacity is wasted in silences; internet voice calls accept packet switching with buffering and prioritisation because it is much cheaper.

analysisChains.title: Why every packet needs a sequence number and a hop limit
steps: Packets from one message are routed independently and can overtake each other
Without a sequence number the receiver could not put them back in order or tell which one is missing
Routing tables change and can briefly contain loops, so a packet might circle between routers
A TTL that every router decreases makes sure such a packet is discarded instead of wasting bandwidth for ever
analysisChains.evaluation: These header fields are the cost of letting each packet travel independently; circuit switching needs neither, because the fixed path keeps the data in order and cannot loop.

examTips: Circuit switching: say 'a dedicated circuit is established before transmission and released at the end' and 'all data follows the same route using the whole bandwidth'.
Packet switching: say 'message split into packets', 'each packet routed independently', 'reassembled at the destination using sequence numbers'.
Security is a mark point both ways: circuit switching uses one route, so it is easier to intercept; packet switching sends packets by different routes, so it is harder to intercept.
Do not just write 'faster'. Circuit switching earns marks for fixed data rate, order of arrival and no reassembly; packet switching loses marks for reassembly time and delays.
Router, one mark per step: reads the destination IP address in the header; looks it up in the routing table; decides the next hop/best route; forwards the packet.
For suitability, link the property to the need, e.g. 'email is not real-time, so packets arriving out of order and being reassembled does not matter'.
For 'how a message crosses the internet' finish the story: packets reordered by sequence number, missing packets identified and a resend request sent, message reassembled.
commonMistakes: Saying that in packet switching all packets follow the same route; each is routed independently and routes can differ.
Saying the router reassembles the message; routers only forward packets, and reassembly happens at the destination host.
Thinking the whole message is resent when one packet is lost; only the missing or corrupted packet is resent.
Describing circuit switching as a physical wire between the two users; it is a chain of reserved links through switching nodes, and capacity on shared media can be reserved.
Justifying a choice with speed ('circuit switching is faster') instead of bandwidth, delay, order or efficiency.
Saying the TTL is a time in seconds that runs out; in practice each router simply subtracts one and discards the packet at zero.
Claiming circuit switching cannot carry data; it can, for example over a leased line.

quickRecall.question: What is circuit switching?
quickRecall.answer: A dedicated path is established between sender and receiver before transmission, used only by them for the whole communication, then released.

quickRecall.question: List the stages of a circuit-switched transfer.
quickRecall.answer: Sender identifies the receiver; network checks the receiver is ready; links are established to form the circuit; data transferred; links released.

quickRecall.question: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of circuit switching.
quickRecall.answer: Benefits: dedicated bandwidth; data arrives in order with a steady delay. Drawbacks: set-up time before sending; bandwidth wasted when idle, and the connection is lost if a link fails.

quickRecall.question: What is packet switching?
quickRecall.answer: The message is split into packets that are sent independently over a shared network, possibly by different routes, and reassembled at the destination.

quickRecall.question: State four items in a packet header.
quickRecall.answer: Source IP address, destination IP address, sequence number, checksum (also hop limit/TTL, packet length).

quickRecall.question: What does a router do with each packet?
quickRecall.answer: Reads the destination IP address, uses its routing table to choose the next hop, decreases the TTL (discarding the packet at zero) and forwards it.

quickRecall.question: How does the receiver cope with packets arriving out of order?
quickRecall.answer: It buffers them and uses the sequence numbers to put them back in the original order before reassembling the message.

quickRecall.question: What happens when a packet is lost?
quickRecall.answer: Its acknowledgement never reaches the sender, which times out and resends that packet only.

quickRecall.question: Give two benefits and two drawbacks of packet switching.
quickRecall.answer: Benefits: bandwidth shared efficiently with no set-up; packets rerouted around failures. Drawbacks: packets can arrive out of order and need reassembly; variable delay and loss under congestion make it less suitable for real-time use.

quickRecall.question: Which method suits a live video conference, and which suits email?
quickRecall.answer: Circuit switching for the video conference (real-time, steady delay, in order); packet switching for email (not real-time, bursty, can be reassembled).
